title: Ship of Fools
author: Russo, Richard Paul
review:
This isn't exactly what I expected but it was quite good. A lot more emphasis on subtle characterization and some interpersonal politics along with interweaving religion and faith with the alien aspects. It did deliver on the reputation it has of sci-fi horror and exploring spooky alien ships but this wasn't really the focus which was a little unexpected.

A lot of the mystery and clues don't really lead anywhere or we don't get clear answers so it's very open ended, could sort of be a negative but I think this lends to the idea of certain beings that we can't truly understand, some interesting things to think about, but I definitely won't obsess over anything unresolved. Some good character moments.

Good depiction of just how alien other life forms might be and the horror creeping in of something inescapable. The pacing is good and the short chapters kept things fresh and the writing style of first person retrospective was effective, I recommend giving it a shot.

highlights.text: I have never wished to hide my differences. I prefer to celebrate them.
Something should have been said, something should have been asked, but I couldn’t imagine what it would be.
Mysteries we did find, and they were many. But I learned that something can be too mysterious, too alien—so mysterious or alien as to approach being meaningless:

I’d been born a freak, abandoned by my parents, raised by committee, taunted and harassed by other children, and shunned by adults. I’ve never been psychologically healthy, and I never will be. I feel a sense of accomplishment because I have managed to achieve a certain level of functionality.

But I knew that to attribute to the alien ship an abstract concept such as Evil, to somehow infuse this dead, inanimate object with that quality and blame our own psychological and emotional failings on it, was absurd. At the same time, I recognized that it was also absurd to deny that something extraordinary was occurring among those who had explored the ship, and that its effects were often devastating.
“What does it smell like?” I asked. “What?” “Evil.” He gave me that faint smile again. “Like unwashed flesh and bodily wastes.”

“There are worlds out there,” I said, gesturing expansively with my right hand, “worlds we haven’t seen in centuries, if ever. Worlds with millions, billions of people, huge thriving cities of advanced civilization, powered by wonders of technology, and with the resources to explore the alien starship in a way we never can. All we need to do is find one of those worlds.” “Yes,” the bishop said, nodding and smiling. “That should be an easy task.”

There is no real free will if God intercedes to protect us or save us from the consequences of our own or other people’s actions and choices. We have to face those consequences ourselves. That is the price we pay for free will.”

“For we can also love and comfort one another, we can choose good over evil, we can relish and appreciate life, we can revel in all the small, wonderful pleasures of being alive, we can love and be loved, and those things are all the greater because they are freely chosen. Because we are not puppets.”
“I’ve wanted to tell you this many times over the years, and I’m going to tell you now. Sometimes, you have the brains of a carrot.
Nikos finished his drink. “After all these years,” he said, “there really isn’t much to say, is there?”
“It doesn’t matter what they think, or what they plan to do. This is the only hope we’ve got.”

I still do not believe—not in an afterlife, not in heaven and hell, and I do not believe in the existence of God. And yet . . . and yet she is still with me in a strange and mysterious way—through my memories of her, through my imagination. I talk to her, I imagine what her replies would be, and I talk further with her. I have long, internal conversations, discussions and even arguments; they sometimes bring me comfort, ease my grief, my guilt. She would probably say I was praying, and perhaps I am.

I had believed we were about to begin a new life. It didn’t happen then, but we are about to now. Despite everything, I have great hopes for the future. Life is difficult for all of us now, but that will change when we make landfall on Antioch.
And so I end this record with hope and anticipation. An old life ends. A new life begins. Life. That, at least, is something I believe in.
